r: The survey exposes students to civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering topics, teamwork, the design process, using math and computer programs to analyze raw data, and presenting results. Applied tasks — calculation, data analysis, information gathering — map to O*NET's Getting Information and Analyzing Data or Information and are exposed to AI, but engineering design reasoning and problem-framing are lower-exposure critical work that task-exposure research associates negatively with substitution. The course is foundational scaffolding for engineering and engineering-technology majors, carries an ABET-relevant introductory role, and holds a GT-SC2 Natural and Physical Sciences designation placing it in the statutory transfer core. At 24 months the instrumental need to build early engineering orientation and problem-framing is not eroded; AI assists computation, but the course grounds the design-thinking students develop across the accredited sequence. Foundational role and general-education lock hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will handle much introductory calculation, data reduction, and preliminary design exploration, weakening the execution rationale for the course's technical tasks. The instrumental case erodes toward engineering judgment — framing problems, specifying constraints, and verifying that AI-generated candidate solutions are sound — competencies that grow more valuable as models produce output of uneven quality across the jagged frontier. The GT-Pathways Natural Sciences designation and the ABET-relevant introductory role cap erosion at Medium by holding the course structurally in the transfer core and the accredited curriculum across a catalog cycle. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical work is the largest AI-use category, so the calculation content is squarely exposed. The rating rises to Medium: introductory execution automates, but foundational engineering literacy remains instrumentally required, and the general-education lock resists faster substitution.

A decade out, AI is deeply embedded in engineering workflows, handling routine analysis, documentation, and generative design exploration, and the introductory execution rationale is largely eroded. But engineering judgment — problem framing, constraint specification, and verifying that an AI-generated design is safe and sound — remains a necessary human competence this foundational course scaffolds, and ABET's mandated content-hour floors plus the gtPathways transfer designation persist absent accreditor or statutory change. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role and institutional lock-in from reaching High. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical — how introductory engineering is taught under pervasive AI — not whether foundational engineering literacy remains instrumentally necessary. Diffusion data (Census BTOS, adoption still uneven) is the main reason to hedge the timeline rather than the capability trajectory, which capability-trend evidence shows advancing quickly.
CET 1040.d: This course is an introductory engineering course exposing students to a cross section of topics in contemporary civil, electrical and mechanical engineering disciplines to assist them with their education career choices. Students are taught to work in teams, introduced to the design process, utilize math and computer programs to analyze raw data and properly display their results in a presentation to their peers. The history of the engineering profession and its relation to current national, social, industrial, ethical, and international issues and problems will be discussed.

r: This course surveys contemporary civil-engineering sub-disciplines — structural, water resources, geotechnical, infrastructure, and sustainable development — alongside professional ethics, rules, and curriculum orientation. The applied tasks are informational: acquiring, organizing, and interpreting disciplinary knowledge, mapping to O*NET's Getting Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others. Task-exposure research classifies explanatory and reading-centered work as exposed, and AI can already summarize how each civil sub-discipline operates. The restraint is foundational: the catalog frames the course as preparing students to begin their engineering studies, grounding the disciplinary context later required courses assume, within an ABET-relevant program. At 24 months the instrumental need to build early disciplinary orientation is not eroded; AI can explain the field, but the course scaffolds the framing students carry into the accredited sequence. Foundational role holds the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will fluently deliver and tutor introductory civil-engineering-technology content — explaining structural, geotechnical, and water-resources fundamentals and professional norms interactively. Real-deliverable evaluations show models approaching expert parity on document-style outputs, so the information-delivery rationale weakens materially. The instrumental case shifts toward the student's own disciplinary orientation and toward critically evaluating AI-generated explanations of the field. The course's foundational role — establishing context for the ABET-relevant sequence — caps erosion at Medium across a catalog cycle, but there is no GT-Pathways designation or licensure mandate to lock it further. The rating rises to Medium: survey content is increasingly AI-deliverable, yet the foundational framing the course provides remains instrumentally useful to students continuing in the major. How such orientation courses are redesigned around AI is a genuine uncertainty rather than a settled outcome.

A decade out, an AI interlocutor can deliver, contextualize, and update the entire survey of civil-engineering sub-disciplines on demand, and the information rationale is substantially eroded. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical — whether a disciplinary orientation course persists as a discussion-and-mentorship seminar or is absorbed into AI-mediated self-study. Foundational disciplinary literacy remains load-bearing for students entering the accredited major, which caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure gate or transfer designation, nothing locks it harder. Task-exposure research is consistent that explanatory content sits at the exposed frontier, while diffusion evidence (Census BTOS, adoption uneven) is the main reason to hedge the timeline. The rating holds Medium; the caveat is that orientation courses may survive chiefly as forums for professional socialization and judgment even where AI performs the informational work.
CET 1100.d: In this course, students learn a cross-section of topics in contemporary Civil Engineering and its sub-disciplines, including Structural Engineering, Water Resources Engineering, Geotechnical Engineering, Infrastructure Engineering, and Sustainable Development. The course emphasizes fundamental concepts and principles of civil engineering, as well as rules, ethics, and education curricula, preparing students to begin their engineering studies.

r: Students learn drawing and modeling for civil applications using Computer-Aided Design. The applied task is technical drafting and digital modeling, mapping to O*NET's Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices and Working with Computers. This is exposed work: observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical tasks are the largest AI-use category, and productivity studies of tool-assisted production (GitHub Copilot roughly 56% faster) illustrate how software-mediated output accelerates. Yet CAD competence remains a prerequisite substrate — the course is a named prerequisite for Building Structures and feeds the estimating and design sequence — and drawings require domain-correct input a novice must learn to supply and check. At 24 months the instrumental need to build drafting-and-modeling fluency is not eroded; AI accelerates drawing production, but the course grounds the spatial and conventions knowledge downstream courses assume. Foundational role holds the rating at Low.

By 2031, generative and parametric CAD will draft and revise civil drawings from high-level prompts, eroding the manual-production rationale that once justified the course. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying design intent, interpreting conventions and standards, and verifying that AI-generated geometry is correct and buildable — judgment the course still develops. Its prerequisite role in the ABET-relevant sequence caps erosion at Medium: downstream Building Structures and design courses assume this competence, holding it structurally in place across a catalog cycle. Task-exposure research places technical software work at the exposed end of the frontier, so the production tasks automate quickly. The rating rises to Medium: drawing production is increasingly automatable, but the foundational modeling literacy and its prerequisite function keep the course instrumentally necessary within the accredited curriculum for at least the near-to-mid term.

A decade out, AI generates and revises civil drawings and models with minimal manual input, and the drafting-production rationale is largely eroded. The residual competence is supervisory — reading, specifying, and verifying models against site and code reality — which the course scaffolds and which downstream design work still requires. Its prerequisite position in the accredited sequence caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure or transfer mandate, nothing locks it harder. Capability-trend evidence shows tool-mediated production advancing fast, so the hedge is diffusion and pedagogy — how drafting instruction is restructured when models do the drawing — rather than whether the automation arrives. The rating holds Medium: foundational modeling literacy remains instrumentally useful as scaffolding, even as the hands-on production the course historically centered becomes something students direct and check rather than perform.
CET 1215.d: Students are introduced to drawing and modeling concepts used in civil engineering applications via Computer Aided Design (CAD).

r: Students learn building structural components and details and architectural modeling through integrated projects, and are introduced to Building Information Modeling and cross-disciplinary collaboration. The applied tasks — digital modeling, specifying components, and coordinating disciplines — map to O*NET's Drafting and Specifying Technical Devices and Working with Computers. BIM modeling is software-mediated and exposed; observed-usage data shows computer work dominates AI use. But the course is a prerequisite for Construction Estimating and grounds the modeling and coordination literacy the building-industry sequence assumes, within an ABET-relevant program. At 24 months the instrumental need to build BIM and structural-detailing competence is not eroded; AI assists modeling, but the course develops the component knowledge and collaboration practice students apply downstream. The collaboration element is partly interpersonal and less automatable. Foundational role and its prerequisite function hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted BIM tools will auto-generate and clash-check building models and draft structural details, eroding the manual-modeling rationale. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying intent, coordinating trades, and verifying that model output is constructible and code-compliant — competencies the course develops and that gain value as AI produces uneven candidate models. Its prerequisite role in the ABET-relevant sequence caps erosion at Medium, holding it structurally in place across a catalog cycle. Diffusion data (Census BTOS, adoption uneven) suggests BIM automation reaches mid-market practice unevenly, tempering how fast the classroom rationale shifts. The rating rises to Medium: modeling production automates, but the coordination judgment and prerequisite function keep the course instrumentally necessary. The interdisciplinary-collaboration component, being real-time and interpersonal, resists substitution more than the modeling itself.

A decade out, AI-driven BIM platforms handle much model generation, coordination, and detailing automatically, and the manual-modeling rationale is substantially eroded. The residual value is supervisory and collaborative — directing the model, resolving cross-disciplinary conflicts, and verifying constructability — which the course scaffolds and which the building sequence still assumes. Its prerequisite role caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure or transfer mandate, nothing locks it harder. The genuine uncertainty is how BIM instruction is restructured when models self-assemble, and how quickly fragmented construction-industry adoption follows capability — diffusion, not capability, is the binding hedge. The rating holds Medium: foundational modeling-and-coordination literacy remains instrumentally useful as scaffolding for later courses and practice, even as the hands-on modeling that once defined the course becomes something students supervise rather than execute end to end.
CET 2003.d: In this course students learn building structural components and details and architectural modeling through integrated class projects. The students are also introduced to Building Information Modeling (BIM) and to the importance of collaboration between related fields in the building industry.

r: The course examines statics — vectors, forces and moments, force systems and resultants, equilibrium, static friction, section properties, and shear and moment diagrams. The applied task is quantitative mechanical analysis, mapping to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems. Such computation is highly exposed — task-exposure research places mathematicians and quantitative analysts among the most-exposed, and AI solves statics problems fluently. But statics is critical foundational scaffolding: it is prerequisite substrate for Mechanics of Materials, Structural Analysis, Concrete Design, and Soil Mechanics, and errors in structural equilibrium carry life-safety consequences, so oversight strictly requires a human holding this knowledge. At 24 months the instrumental need to build statics competence is not eroded; AI can solve the equations, but the course grounds the physical reasoning and verification judgment every downstream structural course and safe design depends on. Foundational role and verification burden hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will solve and explain statics problems instantly, eroding the work-it-by-hand rationale. But the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant: users outside a model's competence are measurably less accurate with miscalibrated trust, so verifying that an AI equilibrium analysis is physically correct demands exactly the trained reasoning this course builds — a genuine, safety-linked verification burden. Its role as prerequisite substrate for the entire structural sequence, within ABET credit-hour floors, caps erosion at Medium and holds it structurally in place. The rating rises to Medium: analytical execution automates, but the foundational mechanics competence remains instrumentally required to verify AI output and to succeed in dependent courses. The shift is that students increasingly check machine analysis rather than perform it, which raises rather than removes the value of understanding the underlying statics.

A decade out, AI performs and narrates statics analysis effortlessly, and the manual-computation rationale is largely gone. But structural safety depends on humans who can tell when an equilibrium result is wrong, and this course builds the substrate that judgment requires; it remains a hard prerequisite for the structural sequence, and ABET content-hour floors persist absent accreditor change. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role and verification burden from either falling away or rising to High. The uncertainty is pedagogical — how mechanics is taught when computation is free — not whether foundational statics competence remains instrumentally necessary for students who will verify AI-generated structural work. Capability advances quickly, but the binding consideration is that safety-critical verification keeps trained mechanical reasoning load-bearing regardless of solver capability.
CET 2150.d: In this course, students examine principles of statics, studies of vectors, their resolution and composition, forces and moments, force systems and their resultants. It also covers force systems in equilibrium, static friction, introduces section properties, shear and moment diagrams.

r: The course examines the interplay between human activity and the environment — anthropogenic and natural effects on air and water quality — applying physics, chemistry, and biology to natural systems. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Getting Information: modeling environmental processes and interpreting quality data. Quantitative analysis is exposed, and AI competently explains environmental-systems concepts, but the scientific reasoning at the core is work task-exposure research associates negatively with substitution. The course sits in an ABET-relevant sequence and grounds the environmental fundamentals later track courses assume. At 24 months the instrumental need to build environmental-systems literacy is not eroded; AI assists calculation and explanation, but the course develops the applied-science reasoning students carry into impact-assessment and treatment coursework. Foundational role within the accredited program holds the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will fluently model air- and water-quality processes, run calculations, and explain environmental-systems behavior, eroding the analytical-execution rationale. The instrumental case shifts toward framing environmental problems, judging which processes and data matter, and verifying AI-generated analyses against physical and regulatory reality — scientific judgment that gains value as models produce uneven output. Its role in the ABET-relevant sequence caps erosion at Medium, holding it in the accredited curriculum across a catalog cycle. Real-deliverable evaluations (GDPval) show models approaching expert parity on technical documents, so the reporting and analysis tasks are increasingly automatable. The rating rises to Medium: execution automates, but the applied-science reasoning and foundational role keep the course instrumentally necessary. A decade out, AI handles environmental modeling, data interpretation, and technical explanation with little friction, and the analytical-execution rationale is substantially eroded. The residual competence is scientific judgment — problem framing, assumption-checking, and verifying that machine analyses are physically and legally sound — which this foundational course scaffolds for the environmental track. Its position in the accredited sequence caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure or transfer mandate, nothing locks it harder. Task-exposure research consistently places critical scientific reasoning at the protected end of the frontier, which is the main reason the rating does not rise further, while diffusion remains the timing hedge. The rating holds Medium: foundational environmental-science literacy stays instrumentally necessary for students who will direct and verify AI environmental analysis, even as routine modeling and reporting become machine work.
CET 3000.d: In this course, students are exposed to the interplay between humans, our activities, and the environment around us. Over the course of the semester, they will explore anthropogenic and natural effects on air and water quality, how these systems operate and the application of applied sciences (e.g., physics, chemistry, and biology) to the natural world.

r: The course examines construction methods, materials, equipment, and sequencing for buildings, highways, bridges, and infrastructure — site preparation, earthwork, formwork, concrete, wood and steel construction, schedule management, safety, and sustainability. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Getting Information, Scheduling Work and Activities, and Inspecting Materials. Much is knowledge about inherently physical field work that task-exposure research classifies as low-exposure, though schedule and documentation elements are more exposed. The course grounds construction-practice literacy the program's methods-and-management sequence assumes, within an ABET-relevant curriculum, and is a prerequisite or corequisite of Construction Estimating. At 24 months the instrumental need to build construction-methods knowledge is not eroded; AI can explain sequencing and materials, but the course develops the field-grounded judgment students apply in estimating, scheduling, and safety decisions. Foundational role and the physical subject matter hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will draft construction schedules, sequence plans, and materials documentation, and explain methods interactively, eroding the information-delivery rationale. But construction execution is embodied and site-specific, and judging whether an AI-generated sequence or safety plan is workable requires field-grounded knowledge the course builds. Its prerequisite role with Estimating and place in the ABET-relevant sequence cap erosion at Medium across a catalog cycle. Diffusion data (Census BTOS, adoption uneven) is especially relevant in fragmented construction, where automation reaches practice slowly. The rating rises to Medium: planning and documentation tasks automate, but the field-grounded methods judgment and foundational role keep the course instrumentally necessary. The safety dimension in particular sustains a verification burden, since a mis-sequenced or unsafe plan has high, sometimes non-obvious, cost that a knowledgeable human must catch.

A decade out, AI competently generates construction schedules, method statements, and materials analyses, and the information-and-planning rationale is substantially eroded. The residual competence is field judgment — recognizing when a plan is unbuildable or unsafe and verifying machine output against site reality — which the course scaffolds and which the construction-management sequence assumes. Its prerequisite role caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure or transfer mandate, nothing locks it harder. Because the underlying work is physical and locally variable, task-exposure research keeps it off the most-exposed list, and slow, uneven construction-industry adoption is the main timing hedge. The rating holds Medium: foundational construction-methods literacy remains instrumentally useful for students who will direct and verify AI planning tools, even as schedule and document production migrates to machines.
CET 3100.d: Students in this course examine the principles, techniques, and practices used in modern construction projects. Emphasis is placed on understanding common construction methods, materials, equipment, and sequencing involved in civil engineering and construction works such as buildings, highways, bridges, and infrastructure systems. Students explore topics including site preparation, earthwork, formwork, concrete, wood, and steel construction, schedule management and control, and construction safety. Students also examine sustainability considerations in construction operations.

r: Students learn to prepare construction cost estimates — using plans and specifications to perform quantity takeoffs, determine costs, and assemble a lump-sum bid. The applied task maps directly to O*NET's Estimating the Quantifiable Characteristics of Products and Analyzing Data or Information, among the more automatable activities in this batch: takeoff and cost computation are quantitative, task-exposure research places quantitative work at the exposed frontier, and automated-takeoff software is already emerging. But estimates carry financial risk, are checked against reality, and require judgment about scope and conditions the plans do not fully specify. The course is a program requirement paired with Construction Methods within an ABET-relevant curriculum. At 24 months the instrumental need to build estimating competence is not eroded; AI accelerates takeoffs, but the course grounds the scope-and-cost judgment students must supply and verify. Program structure and verification hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted takeoff and estimating tools will quantify plans and generate cost models rapidly, eroding the manual-takeoff rationale. The instrumental case shifts toward scoping judgment, pricing assumptions, and verifying that an AI estimate reflects real site conditions and market costs — a financial verification burden, since underpriced bids are costly though ultimately checkable. Real-deliverable evaluations (GDPval) show models approaching parity on structured document tasks, so the computational core automates. The course's program-requirement role in the ABET-relevant sequence caps erosion at Medium across a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium: takeoff and calculation automate, but the estimating judgment and verification competence keep the course instrumentally necessary. Uneven construction-sector diffusion (Census BTOS) tempers how fast automated estimating displaces the classroom rationale in mid-market practice.

A decade out, AI performs quantity takeoffs and cost modeling from plans with minimal manual effort, and the computational rationale is largely eroded. The residual competence is supervisory — setting scope, challenging pricing assumptions, and verifying machine estimates against site and market reality — which the course scaffolds. Its program-requirement role caps the rating at Medium; absent a licensure or transfer mandate, nothing locks it harder, and estimating's high task-exposure pushes toward, not away from, the ceiling. The binding hedge is diffusion and verification: fragmented construction adoption is uneven, and someone accountable for a bid must still stand behind the number. The rating holds Medium: estimating judgment remains instrumentally useful even as takeoff and calculation become machine work, with genuine uncertainty about how much scoping judgment automates around a human accountable for the bid.
CET 3110.d: Students gain a basic understanding of the methods used to prepare a construction project cost estimate. The students use plans and specifications to do quantity takeoffs to determine costs and assemble a lump sum bid. This course is a prerequisite or corequisite of CET 3100 - Construction Methods and Materials .

r: The course applies economic principles to engineering and personal decisions — cash-flow diagrams, time value of money, present, future, and annual worth, and analysis handling inflation, depreciation, taxes, and risk for comparing alternatives. The applied task is quantitative financial analysis, mapping to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems — highly exposed work that task-exposure research places among the most substitutable, and that AI performs fluently today. But the course carries a General Studies Social and Behavioral Sciences designation locking it into the transfer core, and it is a prerequisite for the senior capstone. At 24 months the instrumental need is not eroded; AI computes worth analyses instantly, but the course grounds the decision framing — choosing alternatives, structuring cash flows, judging assumptions — students apply in capstone and practice. General-education lock and foundational role hold the rating at Low despite high task exposure.

By 2031, AI will perform engineering-economy calculations and sensitivity analyses effortlessly, eroding the computational rationale almost entirely. The instrumental case shifts to framing decisions, selecting and defending assumptions about inflation, risk, and depreciation, and verifying that an AI worth-analysis answers the right question — judgment that grows more valuable as models generate plausible but context-blind numbers. The general-studies designation caps erosion at Medium by holding the course in the transfer core, and its prerequisite role for capstone reinforces the floor. Observed-usage data confirms Computer and Mathematical work is the largest AI-use category, so this content is squarely within the deployed frontier. The rating rises to Medium: calculation automates fully, but decision-framing judgment and the general-education lock keep the course instrumentally necessary across a catalog cycle rather than obsolete.

A decade out, AI executes any time-value or alternative-comparison analysis on demand, and the computational rationale is essentially gone. The residual competence is judgment — structuring the decision, defending assumptions, and verifying that machine output reflects reality — which the course scaffolds, plus the general-studies transfer designation that persists absent statutory change. The rating holds Medium, capped by the general-education lock from rising to High despite the content being among the most exposed in the batch. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical: whether engineering economy survives as a judgment-and-communication course when the arithmetic is free. Capability trends make the calculation trivially automatable well within the horizon, so the binding consideration is institutional — the transfer mandate and prerequisite role — rather than any residual difficulty in the computation itself.
CET 3120.d: This course covers the application of economic principles to both engineering and personal economic decision- making. Students in this course are introduced to cash flow diagrams as well as the time value of money concepts of present worth, future worth, and annual worth. This course covers various economic analysis techniques for the comparison and selection of competing economic alternatives. Topics on the proper handling of inflation, depreciation, taxes, and risk are described.

r: The course covers strength of materials — stresses and strains under tension, compression, torsion, and shear; flexural and shearing stresses in beams; principal stresses; deflection; columns; and indeterminate structures — with a laboratory conducting axial, shear, and bending tests. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Inspecting Materials. The analysis is highly exposed, but the lab component is embodied bench work, and the subject is critical foundational scaffolding — a prerequisite for Structural Analysis, Concrete Design, and Soil Mechanics — where errors carry life-safety consequences, so oversight strictly requires a human holding this knowledge. Foundational role, lab embodiment, and verification burden hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will compute stress, strain, deflection, and indeterminate-structure analyses fluently, eroding the manual-calculation rationale. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role, lab embodiment, and verification burden. The uncertainty is how much bench testing is retained pedagogically when analysis is free, not whether foundational material-behavior competence stays instrumentally necessary for students who will verify AI structural work. Capability advances quickly, but safety-critical verification and the embodied laboratory keep trained mechanics reasoning load-bearing regardless of solver capability.
CET 3135.d: This course introduces the theory of strength of materials, stresses, and strains in members subjected to tension, compression, torsion, and shear. Flexural and shearing stresses in beams, principal stresses, and deflection of beams, column analysis, and indeterminate structures are also introduced. The laboratory component of the course is structured to give students experience in the use of laboratory equipment for conducting axial loading, shear and bending tests on various materials.

r: The course introduces structural-analysis theory and applications for statically determinate and indeterminate trusses, beams, and frames, including modeling structures for computer analysis. The applied task is quantitative structural analysis, mapping to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Working with Computers — highly exposed work, and the course explicitly teaches use of structural software that AI increasingly automates. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role and verification burden from falling to Low or rising to High. The uncertainty is how structural pedagogy adapts when modeling is automated, not whether the competence to verify AI structural analysis stays instrumentally necessary. Capability trends make the analysis fast and cheap, so the binding consideration is that safety-critical verification keeps trained structural reasoning load-bearing regardless of how capable the modeling software becomes.
CET 3170.d: In this course, students are introduced to the theory and applications of structural analysis as it applies to various statically determinate and indeterminate trusses, beams, and frames. Students are also introduced to the modeling of such structures for a computer analysis.

CET 3185.d: This course covers and studies the engineering applications of physical properties of ideal fluids, real fluids, hydrostatics, kinematics, energy considerations, momentum principle, dimensional analysis, and incompressible flow in pipes and ducts.

The rating rises to Medium: drafting automates, but the competence to scope, review, and defend an impact assessment against legal challenge remains instrumentally necessary. The uncertainty is how much regulatory-compliance judgment automates around a human who must still sign and defend the document.

A decade out, AI generates full draft environmental impact statements on demand, and the drafting rationale is largely eroded. Because impact statements are contested in court, the verification burden does not disappear with better drafting; it is the reason the rating stays at Medium rather than rising to High despite the content sitting squarely at the exposed writing frontier. The genuine uncertainty is how legal and regulatory institutions treat AI-drafted assessments, not whether capable drafting arrives. The rating holds Medium: the competence to produce a defensible impact statement remains instrumentally useful even as the prose becomes machine-generated.
CET 3320.d: This course is a study of the physical and legal requirements of the environmental impact assessment process. Students will learn to do information research and prepare a draft environmental impact statement.

r: The course introduces reinforced-concrete design to the ACI Code — flexural analysis and design of beams and one-way slabs, serviceability, bond and development lengths, and shear and diagonal tension. The uncertainty is how much routine design automates around a still-accountable engineer, not whether the competence to verify AI concrete design remains instrumentally necessary. Capability advances quickly, but life-safety verification and the licensure-backed stamp keep trained structural-design reasoning load-bearing regardless of how capable the design software becomes.
CET 4120.d: This course is a basic introduction to the fundamental principles of reinforced concrete design according to current American Concrete Institute (ACI) Code.
